title: Gertrude the Great (16 November)
hook: a German nun whose visions centered on the heart of Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Margaret, the queen who fed orphans before she ate. Your line was first the poor. Who got their share before you? Day one thousand forty-three.

At the Last Supper, John's Gospel gives a small, close detail: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." A head resting on a chest. Close enough to hear a heartbeat. The Gospel says nothing more about it. Long afterward, a nun in a German monastery wondered about exactly that. If the beloved disciple was that close, why didn't he write down what he heard? Today's word is the nun who asked, and the answer she wrote.
screen: `A HEAD ON JESUS'S CHEST.` → `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR A HEARTBEAT.` → `A NUN ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Gertrude lived in the monastery of Helfta, in Germany, a house of women known for learning. She came there as a child and grew up among books. She loved study, Latin, the classics, and by her own account she loved them a little too much. Then, she writes, Christ came to her in a vision, gently, and she turned from being a scholar who happened to pray to someone whose whole life was prayer. She wrote down what she received in a book usually called The Herald of Divine Love, and some of it was written by her sisters from what she told them. At the center of it is the heart of Christ. Not as a symbol on a card, but as a place: a home she could rest in, a fire, a fountain. In one of her visions, on the feast of John, she rests near the beloved disciple and asks him the question from the hook. You leaned on that chest. You heard that heart. Why did you write nothing about it? And John, in her vision, answers that his task was to speak of the Word, for the early Church. The sweetness of those heartbeats, he says, was saved for a later time, when the world had grown cold and needed warming. Some readers see in Gertrude an early voice of the devotion that Catholics later called the Sacred Heart. Whatever the history, her point is simple. For her, God's love isn't only an idea. It has a pulse. Heart, in her writing, means the place where God's love and a person's love meet.
screen: `HELFTA, A HOUSE OF LEARNING.` · `FROM SCHOLAR TO A LIFE OF PRAYER.` · `THE HEART AS A HOME.` · `SAVED FOR A COLDER TIME.` · then, large: `IT HAS A PULSE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: pray from the heart, or simply listen to it. Settle, and breathe. Rest a hand on your chest and find your own heartbeat. Let it set the pace for a while. No words needed. If you pray, you can rest there the way Gertrude pictured John resting, and let any words come slowly, or not at all. If you don't, just stay with the beat under your hand for two minutes, and notice the life that's been keeping time for you all along. The bell holds the time.
Gertrude. A nun of Helfta in Germany whose visions, written in The Herald of Divine Love, center on the heart of Christ.

Your line: the heart. That closes a week of saints: Luke the physician, Claret the weaver, Simon and Jude, Josaphat, Albert, Margaret, and now Gertrude. Today, once, put your hand over your heart and pause before you answer someone. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Gertrude on 16 November; Benedictine and Cistercian communities read from her writings, and some Catholics pray her prayers as part of devotion to the Sacred Heart.
